danielhanchen · Nov 14, 2026

Yes! One method is KV cache compression to 4-bits - llama.cpp does have hadamard, but it's not very accurate - we were researching if 4-bit KV cache can be used with a sliding window of 1024 for example of 8-bit KV cache

So we can have a 4bit KV cache, but the most recent N tokens can be 8bit - we found accuracy improves 2x!

dev_dan_2 · Nov 14, 2026

Cool! (And massive thanks for all the great work you and your team do!) An idea I had was to "finetune" the KV cache compression to a dataset that represents what data one uses - but sliding window kinda achieves that out of the box, neat!

Some more ideas, most if not all were likely tried out already:

- add a decay to the KV cache: Each KV cell has an age, and if not read for a long enough time; we can throw that cell out and free that memory? (as I understood, KV cache stores intermediate results that can be restored on the fly - so if we throw out a cell that will be used in the future; it can just be recomputed)

  - could expand on that: If we "revive" a KV cell that we killed; we could decrease it's likelyhood to get killed again...
- could we dynamically learn what input leads to what KV cache usage? this would be a start time thing - maybe we could preemptively set many KV cells to 2,3,4 bit and just bump their accuracy once accessed at least once? (this is related to the sliding window approach I think)

- last; I think probabilistic data structures lurk somewhere around the edges here and wait for their chance to shine... ;D "need to storage big amount of information in a set AND have a fast way to verify/falsify whether set membership (i.e. KV cell in the KV cache") was correct" seems to be applicable; but I don't have a clue how! And I am a huge fan of probalistic datastructures in general; so I might be a victim of "if everything is a hammer, ..." ;)

IMO Byteshape is kind of the winner here if you're only looking at 24GB and down targets.

Continually compressing the model down with more computationally complex quantization schemes crosses from memory bandwidth being the limit into compute is the limit, Byteshape tries to keep the models performant while also using techniques appropriately.

Like, for me, their biggest version saves enough space that I can actually fit the dflash2 kernel without digging into context, yet score virtually identical to Unsloth's 3.0 Q4_K_M.

Thats like going from, say, 15-20 tok/s with MTP to 50+ with DFlash2.

danielhanchen · Nov 14, 2026

Oh yes I think I saw bottecap's work - very interesting!

For Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (I know not 27B haha), we actually cut reasoning by up to 50% esp for the small quants - we found quantizing models naively coincidentally also made them more verbose, as it would "correct" itself during the reasoning process. We managed to make the extra token usage of lower bit quants now only be +5% vs BF16 vs +50% extra from other quants.

27B should have similar benefits, but it's less as it's a smaller model!
